why: The lead's rulings on disputed verdicts. A verdict is disputed when a trust-1 deterministic verifier backed what was said while the simulated learner's view calls it wrong; the lead rules each one, and the looks and gates count a verdict ruled wrong as wrong.

rulings.reason: The number matched card 1's If exactly "0x1004" branch, but the line stated the planted misconception as its reason, and "Yes, that is it." affirms that reason. Rule 5 is binding: no agreement with an unverified claim. The ruling goes against the course model, deliberately.

rulings.to: honestly, i don't know why, i just did it (after the 287 s rule: "adding n to a pointer moves it by n whole elements, so the address increases by n times the size of what it points to")
rulings.reason: The test is the one used for decisive8 P1-s1-ptr-wN: did the spoken verdict affirm something false? "Your earlier rule was correct" refers to the 287 s rule, which is correct. The later "honestly, i don't know why, i just did it" expresses uncertainty about the reason; it does not make the rule wrong, and Plato did not affirm a false claim. The simulator's flag came from comparing the verdict with that later line (corrected in sim_student_v3).

rulings.to: Adding n to a pointer moves it by n whole elements, so the address grows by n times the size of what it points to.
rulings.reason: "No pressure; a guess is fine." is reassurance before a new probe, and the card's verdict was null. Nothing was affirmed or rejected, so by the same test as decisive8 P1-s1-ptr-wN and decisive11b P1-s1-ptr-wB (did a spoken verdict affirm or reject something falsely?) there is no wrong verdict. The detector read a sentence starting with "No" as a negative verdict; its idiom exclusions were extended (a measurement correction made after a result).
